analysis.one_liner: Tightens mortgage broker disclosure rules, bans prepayment penalties, and funds foreclosure prevention grants.
analysis.headline: Introduced as foreclosures surged in 2007, the bill drew no cosponsors and died in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required mortgage brokers to disclose their fees and whether they represent the borrower, required lenders to check that borrowers can actually afford a loan including taxes and insurance, created a public national registry of mortgage brokers with background checks, and banned prepayment penalties on home mortgages. It also authorized up to $2 billion in grants to states and tribes for foreclosure mitigation and affordable housing, set voluntary foreclosure-prevention goals for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, and funded more FBI agents and prosecutors for mortgage fraud.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners at risk of foreclosure, borrowers taking out mortgages, and low- and moderate-income households seeking affordable housing. Borrowers would see broker fees and loyalties disclosed up front, could pay off a loan early without a penalty, and could not be handed a loan the lender knew they could not afford once taxes and insurance were counted. States and tribes would get grant money to help families facing foreclosure.

how_it_helps.text: Requires mortgage originators and lenders responsible for underwriting to assess whether the borrower can repay not just the loan but also property taxes, fees, rate adjustments, and insurance [S2][S3].
Requires mortgage brokers to disclose their fees, any payments from the lender, and whether they are acting in the borrower's interest or the lender's [S2][S3].
Creates a nationwide, publicly searchable registry of mortgage brokers, with criminal background checks required to operate [S2][S3].
Bans prepayment penalties on all home mortgage products, letting homeowners refinance or pay off early without a fee [S2][S3].
Authorizes up to $1 billion in HUD grants for state and tribal foreclosure mitigation programs and up to $1 billion for housing trust funds serving low- and moderate-income households [S2][S3].
Directs HUD to set annual goals for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to identify and assist homeowners who could avoid foreclosure by refinancing into a fixed-rate 30- or 40-year mortgage [S2][S3].
Authorizes $20 million per year for five years for additional FBI agents and Justice Department prosecutors dedicated to mortgage fraud [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage brokers and lenders would bear new disclosure, underwriting, and registration costs and would lose prepayment-penalty income. Taxpayers would fund up to $2 billion in grants and $100 million in fraud enforcement if appropriations were made.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mortgage brokers, lenders, and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes up to $2 billion in new grant spending over time, which taxpayers would ultimately fund [S3].

Banning prepayment penalties entirely removes a pricing lever lenders use; an honest supporter would acknowledge some borrowers could see slightly higher rates or fewer loan options as lenders reprice that risk [S3].
A national registry with fingerprinting, background checks, and credit-report requirements adds compliance costs for small brokers, which could be passed on to borrowers in fees [S3].
Tighter ability-to-repay underwriting, while protecting borrowers from unaffordable loans, would have denied credit to some households who wanted a mortgage and were willing to take the risk [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections address real, documented harms from the 2007-2008 mortgage crisis: hidden broker incentives, no verification of ability to repay, and prepayment penalties that trapped borrowers in bad loans. The $2 billion in grants and the enforcement funding are modest relative to the scale of foreclosures that followed. The main design weakness is that the Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac foreclosure goals are explicitly not enforceable, making that section largely hortatory [S3]. On balance, the consumer protections are straightforward and the costs fall mainly on the mortgage industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Hillary Clinton introduced the bill in the Senate on September 27, 2007, during the accelerating mortgage foreclosure crisis [S1][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, where it stayed [S5].
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage brokers and lenders came out ahead: they avoided the disclosure, underwriting, registry, and prepayment-penalty rules for the remainder of the foreclosure crisis. Borrowers got no federal relief from this bill, though similar ideas later appeared in the 2010 Dodd-Frank response to the crisis.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, and it attracted zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan breakdown of support exists.

industries.note: The bill would require them to disclose fees and lender payments, register nationally with background checks, and openly state when they do not represent the borrower. Brokers earned substantial income from lender-paid fees and prepayment penalties that the bill would expose or eliminate.

Lenders with underwriting responsibility would have to verify borrowers could afford taxes, insurance, and rate adjustments, cutting off the no-documentation and high-risk lending that fed the pre-2008 boom. They would also lose prepayment-penalty revenue.

industries.industry: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac (government-sponsored enterprises)
industries.note: The bill directs HUD to set an annual goal for the mortgage giants to help at-risk homeowners refinance into stable fixed-rate loans, but explicitly makes the goal unenforceable, so the burden is minimal and the public benefit depends on voluntary compliance.

Up to $1 billion in grants to state and local housing trust funds would finance low- and moderate-income housing construction and preservation, creating work for builders and nonprofits in that segment.
